title: Serving many LoRA adapters on one base model
summary: Serve hundreds of fine-tunes from one base: merge vs unmerged, Punica's SGMV, S-LoRA's unified paging and tensor parallelism, vLLM and LoRAX knobs, cluster routing, cold starts and capacity planning.
outcomes: Explain why separate per-fine-tune deployments waste both memory and decode batching
Choose between merged, merge-and-swap and unmerged adapter serving for a given traffic mix
Explain how SGMV batches rows for different adapters and why distinct adapters cost bandwidth
Compute adapter memory and its KV-cache equivalent, and explain S-LoRA's unified paging
Configure max_loras, max_lora_rank and max_cpu_loras in vLLM and predict their memory cost
Explain how S-LoRA and vLLM shard adapters under tensor parallelism and why the extra communication stays rank-sized
Compare routing, merge switching, cold-start and fairness policies for serving adapters across GPUs and tenants
Build a mixed-adapter layer, size a deployment from a workload and generate an S-LoRA-style benchmark trace

lessons.title: Why serving one model per fine-tune wastes GPUs

blocks.md: Picture a platform where 100 customers each fine-tuned the same 7B base model with LoRA (all linear layers, rank 16, as in the LoRA course). Every customer wants an endpoint. The obvious plan is to merge each adapter into the base weights and deploy 100 independent models. The Punica paper (Chen et al. 2023, from the University of Washington and Duke), which built a system for serving many LoRA models on a shared GPU cluster, describes the cost: if one model needs $k$ GPUs, $n$ fine-tunes served this way need $k \times n$ GPUs, ignoring that they all share 99% of their weights.

Memory makes this concrete. With Llama-2-7B's shape (6.74B parameters, 16-bit), one merged copy is 13.5 GB (2 bytes per parameter), so 100 copies are 1.35 TB. The adapters themselves are tiny: rank 16 on all seven linear layers of 32 layers is 40.0M parameters, 80 MB in 16-bit. One base plus 100 adapters is 21.5 GB.

Where does 40.0M come from? The seven linear layers in each block are the attention query, key, value and output projections and the MLP's gate, up and down projections. A rank-16 adapter on a matrix with $p$ inputs and $q$ outputs adds 16 times the sum $p + q$ numbers, 16 rows of A plus 16 columns of B: 131,072 for each 4096 by 4096 attention projection and 241,664 for each 4096 by 11,008 MLP projection. That is 1,249,280 per layer, and 32 layers give 39,976,960, about 40.0M.

blocks.title: Weight memory for 100 fine-tunes of a 7B model

scenes.caption: Merging every adapter duplicates the 13.5 GB base 100 times: 1,348 GB of weights before any KV cache.
Keeping adapters separate stores the base once: 13.5 GB + 100 x 80 MB = 21.5 GB. Even 1,000 adapters (93.5 GB) take about as much as 7 merged copies (94 GB).

blocks.md: Memory is only half the waste. Recall from the inference course that each **decode step** reads all the weights to produce one token per sequence, so it is limited by memory bandwidth, not arithmetic. Batching many sequences into one step shares that weight read. Punica's measurements (Figure 1) show that going from batch 1 to batch 32 raised the decode step from 11 ms to 13 ms for short sequences (17 ms to 34 ms for long ones). Thirty-two times the tokens for a small fraction more time.

Separate models split the traffic. If 100 endpoints each see a trickle of requests, each one decodes at batch size 1 to 3 and pays nearly the full weight read per token. Punica reports exactly this for baseline systems: with each request on a distinct LoRA model they ran at batch size 1, and with mixed popularity mostly at batch sizes of 1 to 3.

scenes.caption: One model per fine-tune: three full copies, each decoding its own tiny batch, each paying the full weight read per step.
Shared base: all requests join one batch over a single copy of the base weights, and each request adds its own small LoRA term. This is multi-LoRA serving.

blocks.md: LoRA fine-tunes share a frozen base. A server that keeps the base once and batches requests for different adapters together gets both the memory saving and the batching efficiency that separate deployments throw away.

blocks.question: 100 merged 7B fine-tunes would fit on a large cluster. Why is serving them as separate models still inefficient when each gets little traffic?
options: Merged models are slower per token than the base model
Each model decodes tiny batches, so most of each weight read serves only one or two tokens
Merged weights cannot use the KV cache
The adapters must be recomputed for every token
blocks.explain: Decode is bandwidth bound: the cost of a step is dominated by reading the weights, and batching shares that read. Splitting traffic across 100 copies leaves each with batch sizes near 1, so GPU time per token stays high.

blocks.question: You host 50 rank-16 all-linear adapters (80 MB each, 16-bit) for one 7B base. How much memory do the adapters take, compared with the base?
options: About 4 GB, under a third of the 13.5 GB base
About 40 GB, three times the base
About 400 MB, negligible
About 675 GB, the same as 50 merged copies
blocks.explain: 50 x 80 MB = 4.0 GB. That is real memory, which matters later when adapters compete with the KV cache, but it is small next to 50 x 13.5 GB = 675 GB for merged copies.

lessons.title: Merge, swap, or compute the adapter on the fly

blocks.md: With one base in memory there are two ways to apply adapters. Recall from the LoRA course: $W_0$ is the frozen pretrained weight, and an adapter is the product $BA$ of two thin rank-$r$ matrices, where $A$ maps the input down to $r$ numbers and $B$ maps them back up. **Merge and swap**: the LoRA paper's suggestion is to fold an adapter into the base, $W = W_0 + BA$ (with the LoRA course's scaling $s$ folded into $B$), serve it, and to switch tasks subtract $BA$ and add $B'A'$. **Unmerged**: keep $W_0$ untouched and compute each request's adapter term on the fly, which S-LoRA (Sheng et al. 2023, a serving system from UC Berkeley and Stanford built to serve thousands of LoRA adapters at once) writes as:

blocks.caption: S-LoRA Eq. 2. Here h is the layer's output for input row x and W is the base weight. Their A is input width by r and B is r by output width, the transpose of the LoRA paper's naming. The xW part is shared by every request; xAB is per request.

blocks.md: Merging is free per token but serves one adapter at a time, because a merged weight bakes one adapter into every row of the batch. A batch that mixes requests for adapters A, B and C needs each row multiplied by a different weight, which only the unmerged form allows. With a batch $X$ whose row $i$ is one request's current token vector and uses adapter $a(i)$:

blocks.tex: Y = X W_0 + \begin{bmatrix} x_1 A_{a(1)} B_{a(1)} \\ x_2 A_{a(2)} B_{a(2)} \\ \vdots \end{bmatrix}
blocks.caption: Y equals X times W0 for all rows at once, plus, for each row i, that row times the A and B of its own adapter a(i). One big matmul for the base, plus a different small low-rank product per row.

blocks.md: The extra cost is small in arithmetic. Per token, a rank-16 adapter on a 4096 by 4096 projection costs $16 \times (4096 + 4096)$ multiply-adds (16 x 4096 to shrink the input through A, then 16 x 4096 to expand it back through B), which is 131,072, against $4096^2$ = 16,777,216 for the base: 0.78%. S-LoRA's argument is that this overhead is far smaller than what batching the base matmul across all adapters saves.

blocks.title: Toy schedule: 3 adapters, each with 1 request of 4 tokens

scenes.caption: Merge and swap serves adapters one after another. Assumed costs: 12 ms per decode step, 10 ms to unmerge one adapter and merge the next.
Unmerged: A, B and C decode in the same batch. Each step costs a little more (assumed 14 ms with three LoRA add-ons), but all three finish at 56 ms and nobody waits for a swap.

Simplified: real step times depend on batch size, sequence length and kernels. The shape of the result is what S-LoRA measured: merging wins with one adapter, and its throughput declines once more than two adapters are active.

blocks.prompt: S-LoRA compared its unmerged design with a merge-based variant (merge the current adapter before each batch, switch when too many requests wait). With exactly one adapter, which design gives higher throughput?
blocks.reveal: **The merged variant.** S-LoRA's ablation (Figure 9), an experiment that changes one design choice and keeps everything else fixed, shows merging wins with one adapter, because it pays the merge once and then runs with no LoRA computation at all. Its throughput declines once there are more than 2 adapters, because switching leaves the GPU underused. The right choice depends on how many adapters are active at once.

blocks.md: Unmerged does not mean easy. Requests in one batch use adapters with different ranks and different sequence lengths, so padding everything into one batched matmul wastes work. S-LoRA's variant that copies adapters into contiguous memory and uses padded batched matmul (S-LoRA-bmm) was much slower than the version with custom kernels, GPU functions written for exactly this mixed-rank job.

Merge when one adapter dominates the traffic and per-token latency matters most. Keep adapters unmerged when many adapters are active concurrently, so the base matmul can be batched across all of them.

One case overrides that rule: a **quantized base**. Many deployments store the base in 4 bits (QLoRA's NF4 format through bitsandbytes, or the AWQ and GPTQ formats) to save memory, and a QLoRA adapter was trained against those rounded weights. Merging means dequantizing, adding $BA$ and quantizing again, and one 4-bit step is large next to a typical LoRA update, so most of the update is rounded away; the LoRA course's training-recipe lesson measures this. So the adapter stays unmerged, in 16 bits, beside the quantized base, which is exactly the multi-LoRA path. vLLM's quantization example serves LoRA adapters on bitsandbytes (QLoRA), AWQ and GPTQ bases with `enable_lora=True`. If one adapter must be merged for latency, merge it into a dequantized 16-bit copy of the base and pay 16-bit memory for that copy.

blocks.question: Why can a merged LoRA model not serve requests for two different adapters in the same batch?
options: Because merged weights are stored in a different data type
Because merging removes the KV cache
Because the batch would need a different weight matrix for different rows, and a merged model has only one
Because the base model must be reloaded from disk for each adapter
blocks.explain: A matmul applies one weight matrix to every row of the batch. After merging, that matrix contains one specific adapter. Mixing adapters in a batch requires the shared W0 plus a per-row low-rank term, which is exactly the unmerged form.

blocks.question: A support-bot product uses a single LoRA fine-tune and is judged on per-token latency. What should it do?
options: Run an unmerged multi-LoRA server with max_loras (the number of adapters allowed in one batch) set high
Swap the adapter in and out every batch
Serve the base model without the adapter
Merge the adapter into the base weights and serve that model
blocks.explain: With one adapter there is nothing to batch across, so the unmerged add-on is pure overhead. Merging gives the base model's cost per token, which is also what S-LoRA's single-adapter ablation found.

blocks.question: A team serves a 4-bit base with one hot QLoRA-trained adapter. To remove the LoRA overhead they merge the adapter into the 4-bit weights and quantize the result again. What is the likely outcome?
options: Nothing changes: merging is exact in any number format
The merged model loses much of the fine-tune, because requantizing rounds away most of the small update
The KV cache must be recomputed in 4 bits, which slows decode
vLLM refuses to serve a base that was ever merged
blocks.explain: A 4-bit step is coarse compared with a LoRA update, so the round trip turns most of BA into rounding noise. Keep the adapter unmerged in 16 bits beside the quantized base, or merge into a dequantized 16-bit copy and accept its memory cost.

lessons.title: Batching different adapters: Punica's SGMV kernel

blocks.md: Punica (Chen et al. 2023) made the unmerged form fast with one CUDA kernel. CUDA (Compute Unified Device Architecture) is NVIDIA's platform for programming GPUs, and each kernel, the GPU function named in the previous lesson, is launched across thousands of threads, grouped into thread blocks. Punica's kernel is **Segmented Gather Matrix-Vector multiplication (SGMV)**. The trick starts with ordering: sort the requests in a batch so that all rows using the same adapter sit next to each other. A list of segment boundaries $s$ then says which rows belong to which adapter: it holds the first row of each segment plus a final entry equal to the row count, so segment $i$ starts at row $s_i$ and stops just before the next entry, $s_{i+1}$. That explains the name: the batch is cut into segments, each segment gathers its own adapter's weights, and in decode each row is a single token vector, so the work is matrix times vector.

blocks.title: Grouping a decode batch of 8 requests by adapter

scenes.caption: Requests arrive for four different adapters in arbitrary order. A plain batched matmul cannot handle this: each row needs different LoRA weights.
Reorder the batch so equal adapters are contiguous: A A A B B C D D. The base matmul does not care about row order.
Segment starts s = [0, 3, 5, 6, 8]: rows 0 to 2 use adapter A, 3 to 4 use B, 5 uses C, 6 to 7 use D. The kernel reads each adapter's weights once per segment.

blocks.md: Punica's semantics fit in one line of Python-style code: `Y[s[i] : s[i+1]] += X[s[i] : s[i+1]] @ W[i]`. In words: for each segment $i$, take its rows of X, multiply them by that segment's weight, and add the result into the same rows of Y. A LoRA layer calls it twice. **SGMV-shrink** multiplies the hidden-size input by each segment's A, producing an r-dimensional vector per row. **SGMV-expand** multiplies that by each segment's B and adds the result into the base output in place.

blocks.title: A reference version of the two SGMV calls

scenes.caption: The base projection runs once for all 8 rows as an ordinary GEMM. This is the expensive part, and it is fully shared.
Shrink: segment 0 (rows 0 to 2) multiplies by adapter A's 4096 x 16 matrix, giving three 16-dim vectors.
The loop covers every segment. A real kernel does not loop on the host: it launches all segments at once, one group of thread blocks per segment.
Expand: each segment's 16-dim vectors are multiplied by that adapter's 16 x 4096 B and added into y in place.
scenes.output: 8 rows done: 1 base GEMM + 2 SGMV launches

blocks.md: How much does mixing adapters cost? Punica answers with a roofline analysis. The roofline model says a kernel can run no faster than the lower of two limits: the GPU's peak arithmetic rate, or its memory bandwidth times the kernel's **arithmetic intensity**, the floating-point operations (FLOPs) it does per byte it moves. Low intensity means the kernel waits on memory. Punica counts FLOPs and bytes for one SGMV call with $s_n$ rows (the last entry of the boundary list), $n$ distinct adapters and a weight of shape $h_i \times h_o$:

blocks.tex: \text{FLOP} = 2\, s_n h_i h_o \qquad \text{I/O bytes} = 2\,\big[\, s_n (h_i + h_o) + n\, h_i h_o \big]
blocks.caption: Punica Section 7.1. The factor 2 in I/O is 2 bytes per 16-bit value. Reading adapter weights grows with the number of distinct adapters n.

blocks.md: In words: each row multiplies a length-$h_i$ input by an $h_i$ by $h_o$ weight, which is $h_i h_o$ multiply-adds, and a multiply-add counts as 2 FLOPs. The bytes are every row's input and output, $h_i + h_o$ values per row for $s_n$ rows, plus one $h_i \times h_o$ weight per distinct adapter, at 2 bytes per value. Only that last term depends on how many adapters the batch mixes.

Plug in Punica's case study, $h_i = 16$, $h_o = 4096$, 64 rows. The work is 2 x 64 x 16 x 4096 = 8,388,608 FLOPs either way. If all 64 rows share one adapter, the bytes are 2 x (64 x 4,112 + 65,536) = 657,408, so the call does 12.8 FLOPs per byte. If all 64 use different adapters, the weight term becomes 64 x 65,536 and the bytes reach 8,914,944: 0.94 FLOPs per byte, the same as a single row. Both numbers sit far below the A100 ridge of about 153 FLOPs per byte from the basics course, so even the shared case is memory bound (Punica says so for Identical); mixing adapters multiplies the bytes for the same work. The distinct case becomes a pure memory read, which Punica handles with a bandwidth-oriented schedule instead of Tensor Cores, the GPU's dedicated matrix-multiply units, which only pay off when there is plenty of math per byte loaded.

blocks.title: Measured SGMV latency, batch 1 vs 64 (Punica Figure 8)

scenes.caption: One adapter for every row: 37 microseconds at batch 1 and 40 at batch 64. Batching is nearly free.

Skewed popularity reaches 46 microseconds at batch 64. Every row on its own adapter reaches 116 microseconds, because each row reads its own weights. A step makes many such calls, yet Punica's layer benchmark barely changes with the adapter mix.

blocks.md: At the model level the add-on barely matters. Punica reports 1,044 tokens/s for a 7B model whatever the adapter mix, and for a 70B model 441 to 446 tokens/s, while a baseline on vLLM (the open-source serving engine behind PagedAttention) without multi-LoRA support reached about 21 to 25 tokens/s with many adapters (457 tokens/s when serving the backbone, the base model, alone).

blocks.title: Extra weight bytes read per decode step (simplified)

y.label: adapter bytes as % of base weights

scenes.caption: Simplified bandwidth model for the 7B shape: a step reads the 13.5 GB base once plus each distinct adapter once. At rank 16, 32 distinct adapters add 19% more bytes.

At rank 64, 32 distinct adapters add 76%, and 64 adapters more than the base itself. High-rank adapters with many distinct tenants per batch erode the batching win; this model ignores KV cache reads and kernel efficiency.
At rank 8 the same 32 adapters add under 10%. Rank is a serving cost, not only a training choice.

blocks.md: SGMV groups rows by adapter and runs all segments in one launch, so a batch can mix adapters while the base matmul stays shared. Its cost grows with the number of distinct adapters and their rank, because each one's weights must be read.

blocks.question: A batch of 64 decode rows is spread across 64 different adapters. According to Punica's roofline analysis, what limits the SGMV kernel?
options: Tensor Core throughput, because there are 64 matmuls
Memory bandwidth, because each row reads its own adapter weights and does little math per byte
PCIe bandwidth (the CPU-to-GPU bus), because adapters are always loaded from the CPU
Nothing: the cost is identical to one shared adapter
blocks.explain: With n = s_n the I/O term n h_i h_o grows with the batch, so arithmetic intensity stays about 0.94 FLOPs per byte, firmly bandwidth bound. Measured latency rose from 37 to 116 microseconds, versus 37 to 40 for a single shared adapter.

blocks.question: Using the simplified bandwidth model, which change most reduces the extra bytes read per step when 32 distinct adapters share each batch?
options: Raising the batch size to 64
Sorting rows by adapter
Using more prefill tokens per batch
Halving every adapter's rank
blocks.explain: Extra traffic is proportional to (distinct adapters) x rank. Halving the rank halves it. Sorting is required for SGMV to work but does not change how many adapter bytes must be read, and a bigger batch with more tenants can add distinct adapters.

lessons.title: Thousands of adapters: S-LoRA's unified paging and loading

blocks.md: SGMV handles the adapters in a batch. S-LoRA (Sheng et al. 2023) asks the next question: what if there are thousands of adapters and only a few dozen are needed at any moment? Its answer is to keep **all adapters in host (CPU) memory** and copy to the GPU only those used by the currently running batch. The number of adapters is then bounded by host memory, not GPU memory.

Fetching is cheap relative to a decode step. Punica measured loading a LoRA model from host memory over PCIe (PCI Express) Gen4 x16 (the bus between CPU and GPU; generation 4 with 16 lanes moves about 32 GB/s each way) at around 2 ms for a whole adapter (about 50 microseconds per layer; the paper does not give the adapter's rank or target layers), against roughly 30 ms per decode step in its setup, and overlaps the copy with computation. The arithmetic lands in the same range: the course's 80 MB 7B adapter over 32 GB/s takes 80 / 32,000 s, about 2.5 ms. S-LoRA also **prefetches**: while the current batch decodes, it predicts which adapters the waiting queue will need next and loads them early.

The harder problem is GPU memory layout. Recall PagedAttention: the KV cache is split into fixed-size blocks so that requests of different lengths do not fragment memory. Adapters cause the same trouble. They come and go with requests, and their sizes vary with rank. Allocating them contiguously next to a paged KV cache leaves holes.

S-LoRA's observation: in one layer, a request's KV cache has shape $(S, H)$ for $S$ tokens, where $H$ is the hidden size (the model width, 4096 for a 7B Llama), and a LoRA weight has shape $(R, H)$ for rank $R$. Both are stacks of $H$-sized vectors. **Unified Paging** therefore uses one memory pool whose page is a single $H$-vector. A KV tensor of length $S$ takes $S$ pages and an adapter weight of rank $R$ takes $R$ pages, interleaved anywhere in the pool.

blocks.title: A unified pool of 24 pages (toy, one layer)

scenes.caption: One statically allocated pool fills all GPU memory left after the base weights and activations. Each page holds one H-dimensional vector.
Request r1 arrives using adapter X (toy: one rank-4 weight, 4 pages, tone a) and has 3 tokens of KV cache (3 pages, tone d).
Request r2 uses adapter Y with rank 8, so Y takes 8 pages. Different ranks are just different page counts.
r1 generates 2 more tokens; its KV pages land wherever space is free.
r1 finishes. Its KV pages and adapter X (no longer used) are freed, leaving holes. r2 grows by one page.
r3 arrives with adapter Z (rank 2) and 6 tokens. It fills the holes, non-contiguously. Custom kernels read adapters and KV from scattered pages, so no space is lost to fragmentation.

blocks.md: The pool also makes the tradeoff visible: adapter pages and KV pages compete. Per layer, the S-LoRA paper describes LoRA on the four attention matrices. Each factor of a rank-16 adapter on a square H by H matrix is 16 H-vectors, so the adapter is 4 matrices x 2 factors x 16 = 128 pages. Each token stores one key vector and one value vector per layer, 2 pages, so 128 pages equal 64 tokens of keys plus values. For a 7B model with all seven linear layers adapted at rank 16, the 80 MB adapter equals about 152 tokens of KV cache: one token costs 2 vectors x 32 layers x 4096 numbers x 2 bytes = 524,288 bytes, 0.5 MiB (a mebibyte is 2 to the 20 bytes), and 80 MB divided by that is about 152. Every adapter resident on the GPU is a few requests' worth of context that cannot be cached.

Two scheduling policies follow. **Adapter clustering** prefers to batch requests that share adapters, leaving more room for KV cache and bigger batches, at some cost to latency and fairness. **Admission control** drops requests that cannot meet the latency target (S-LoRA's early-abort strategy) instead of letting the whole queue miss it. For decode, S-LoRA uses MBGMV (Multi-size Batched Gather Matrix-Vector multiplication), a version of Punica's kernel extended to mixed ranks (the multi-size part) and non-contiguous pages. Prefill sends many tokens per request, so the work is matrix times matrix, and S-LoRA uses MBGMM, the Matrix-Matrix version, written in Triton, a Python-based language for writing GPU kernels.

blocks.title: Clustering and prefetching from the waiting queue (toy)

scenes.caption: Eight requests wait, labelled by adapter, oldest first. The next batch has room for 4. Each resident rank-16 7B adapter costs 80 MB of the pool, about 152 tokens of KV cache.
First come, first served takes the first 4: A, C, A, B. Three adapters must be resident: 3 x 152 = 456 tokens of KV room spent on adapter pages.

Clustering with d = 2 (S-LoRA's rule): admit in order until the batch has 2 adapters, then prefer requests whose adapter is already in. The batch becomes A, C, A, A: 304 tokens of adapter pages, 152 fewer.
While that batch decodes, S-LoRA looks at what is still waiting (B, D, C, E) and prefetches the adapters it lacks, B and D first, so the next batch does not stall on a host-to-GPU copy.
The cost of clustering: B arrived before the third A but waits a full batch. S-LoRA reports that a small d generally helps throughput, with latency and fairness among adapters as the price.

blocks.title: S-LoRA throughput vs number of adapters (Table 3, setting S2)

scenes.caption: Llama-7B with adapters of ranks 8 to 64, one A100 80GB, 5 adapters. vLLM-packed runs one merged vLLM copy per adapter (2.04 req/s); HuggingFace's PEFT library swaps adapters between batches (0.74).
100 adapters: vLLM-packed runs out of GPU memory (shown as 0). PEFT falls to 0.24 req/s. S-LoRA holds 7.29.
2,000 adapters: S-LoRA still serves 6.71 req/s (6.69 at 1,000). The baselines were out of memory or not run at this scale.

blocks.md: Unified Paging is not magic capacity. Adapter pages and KV pages come from the same pool, so many large adapters active at once shrink the space for KV cache and therefore the batch size. That is why clustering and rank choices still matter.

blocks.question: Why did S-LoRA put adapter weights and KV cache in one paged pool instead of two separate pools?
options: Because both are stacks of H-sized vectors that come and go dynamically, so sharing H-sized pages avoids fragmentation and lets the split between them change with load
Because adapters and KV cache are always the same size
Because the base model weights also need paging
Because PCIe transfers require page-aligned buffers
blocks.explain: A KV tensor is (S, H) and a LoRA weight is (R, H). With pages of one H-vector each, both fit the same allocator, holes left by one can be reused by the other, and the balance shifts automatically between many adapters and long contexts.

blocks.question: A burst of requests touches 40 rarely used adapters at high rank. In S-LoRA's design, what is the most direct cost?
options: The base model must be reloaded
Requests for those adapters must wait for a merge
Adapter pages take space from the KV cache, reducing how many requests fit in a batch, and each adapter must be fetched from host memory
SGMV can no longer batch rows together
blocks.explain: Adapters live in host memory and are fetched on demand into the unified pool. Each active adapter uses pages that the KV cache could have used, so many large ones at once cut the batch size. Nothing is merged, and batching still works.

lessons.title: Multi-LoRA across GPUs: tensor parallelism for adapters

blocks.md: Everything so far fits on one GPU. A 70B base in 16-bit is 140 GB and does not, so it is served with **tensor parallelism** (TP) across $N$ GPUs. Recall from the GPU and inference basics course's tensor-parallel lesson: an MLP's first matrix is split by columns, its second by rows, and one **all-reduce** (every GPU contributes a same-shaped tensor and every GPU receives the elementwise sum) adds the partial results. Attention splits the same way, by heads for Q, K and V and by rows for the output projection. Every adapter must now be split too. The question is how to cut $A$ and $B$ so the adapters add as little communication as possible.

Start with the **column-parallel** layer, the MLP's first matrix $W_1$. Every GPU holds the whole input $X$ and its slice of the output columns. The LoRA term $XA_1B_1$ has the same output width, so $B_1$ is split by columns like $W_1$. But each GPU then needs the full rank-$r$ vector $XA_1$. S-LoRA splits $A_1$ by its $r$ columns too: each GPU computes $r/N$ of the numbers, and an **all-gather** (every GPU contributes a piece, every GPU receives all pieces joined) rebuilds the $r$-vector. With $r = 16$ that is 16 numbers per token, not 4,096.

Then the **row-parallel** layer, $W_2$. Its input arrives split across GPUs, so $A_2$ is split by rows to match, and each GPU's product is a partial $r$-vector; an all-reduce of $r$ numbers sums them. $B_2$ is split by columns, and here is the trick: each GPU adds its slice of $XA_2B_2$ into its own partial sum of the base output, so the base's existing all-reduce delivers the LoRA result too. S-LoRA calls this fusing the all-gather for the last matmul into the final all-reduce. Attention follows the same pattern, with the Q, K and V projections playing $W_1$ and the output projection playing $W_2$.

blocks.title: S-LoRA's split of a LoRA-adapted MLP, as seen by one of N GPUs

scenes.caption: The base alone (Megatron-style): W1 split by columns, W2 by rows, and one all-reduce of an h-sized vector per token to sum the partial outputs.

First LoRA pair (A1, B1, beside W1): A1 split along its rank, so each GPU computes r/N numbers per token; an all-gather of just r values rebuilds the rank vector, and the column slice of B1 adds into the base output (add_1).

Second LoRA pair (beside W2): A2 split by rows to match the split input gives partial rank vectors, summed by an all-reduce of r values. B2's column slice is added into the base's partial sum (add_2).
Only rank-sized tensors cross GPUs for the adapters. The base's existing all-reduce carries the LoRA output too, and no GPU stores a replicated adapter matrix.

blocks.caption: S-LoRA Section 6.2, in elements sent per GPU for B tokens: three all-gathers (Q, K, V) and one all-reduce (output projection) of rank-r tensors, against one all-reduce of hidden-size h tensors.

blocks.md: The coefficients are the usual per-GPU traffic of the two collectives: an all-reduce of $n$ elements moves $2(N-1)n/N$, an all-gather $(N-1)n/N$. Apply the same rule to the MLP (all-gathers for gate and up, an all-reduce for down; S-LoRA writes out only attention) and count bytes per token per layer in 16-bit for the 7B shape. At $N = 2$ the base's two all-reduces move 16,384 bytes and rank-16 adapters add 144 bytes, 0.88%. At $N = 4$: 24,576 against 216, still 0.88%. Rank 64 gives 576 and 864 bytes, 3.5%. For a whole layer the ratio is $9r/(4h)$: it does not depend on $N$, because both sides scale with $(N-1)/N$.

blocks.title: Bytes sent per GPU per token per layer, 7B shape, 16-bit

scenes.caption: The base all-reduces carry h = 4,096 values each; adapters add only rank-sized collectives. Computed from S-LoRA's cost formulas, extended to the MLP by the same rule.
Simplified: bytes are not the whole cost. Each extra collective also pays a fixed latency, which at small batches matters more than its size (the basics course's tensor-parallel lesson).

blocks.md: S-LoRA measured the effect on Llama-30B (2 and 4 A100 40GB GPUs, 10 and 100 adapters) and Llama-70B (2 and 4 A100 80GB, 10 adapters): throughput with and without the LoRA communication differed little, and the LoRA's extra computation cost more than its communication. Going from 2 to 4 GPUs raised throughput by more than 2x, because the system was memory-bound and more GPUs left more room for KV cache.

vLLM implements both choices. By default only half of the LoRA work is sharded: on column-parallel layers $A$ is replicated (every GPU computes the same $r$-vector, no communication) and $B$ is split; on row-parallel layers $A$ is split and $B$ is full size, so each GPU's partial LoRA output rides the base all-reduce. That adds no collectives, but duplicates part of the adapter on every GPU. With `--fully-sharded-loras` vLLM uses S-LoRA's layers (the source cites the paper): every matrix is split, at the price of an all-gather on column layers and an all-reduce of the shrunk vector on row layers. The engine-argument docs say the fully sharded mode is likely faster at high sequence length, max rank or tensor-parallel size.

blocks.prompt: Take the 7B shape at TP = 4 with one rank-16 slot (80 MB unsharded). Roughly how much of that slot does each GPU store in vLLM's default mode, and in fully sharded mode?
blocks.reveal: **About 42 MB by default, 20 MB fully sharded.** Computed from vLLM's slot shapes: in the default mode the column layers (q, k, v, gate, up) keep a full $A$ and the row layers (o, down) keep a full $B$, so a large part of the adapter is replicated. Fully sharded splits every matrix, exactly 80 / 4 = 20 MB. At rank 64 the numbers are 168 and 80 MB. Replicated slots also mean replicated shrink and expand work, which is why the gap grows with rank and TP size.

blocks.code:
# Not run here (no NVIDIA GPU on this machine). Adapted from the vLLM docs.
vllm serve meta-llama/Llama-2-70b-hf \
    --tensor-parallel-size 4 \
    --enable-lora --fully-sharded-loras \
    --max-loras 8 --max-lora-rank 64 \
    --lora-modules sql=/adapters/sql chat=/adapters/chat
blocks.caption: A 70B base on 4 GPUs with fully sharded adapters. Benchmark both modes on your own traffic: the docs give a direction, not a threshold.

blocks.md: Do not shard an adapter the way you would shard an independent layer. Splitting $B_1$ by rows, for example, leaves each GPU with a partial full-width output (all $d$ columns, before the split) that needs its own all-reduce of $d$ values: the expensive collective the scheme exists to avoid. Align each factor's split with the base matrix it sits beside.

Under tensor parallelism, split each adapter so its splits line up with the base: A along the rank (column layers) or rows (row layers), B along the output columns. Only rank-sized vectors cross GPUs, and the last result rides the base all-reduce.

blocks.question: In S-LoRA's scheme, why is the extra communication for rank-16 adapters under 1% of the base's, at any TP degree?
options: Adapters are only applied on GPU 0
The adapter collectives move rank-sized vectors (16 values per token) while the base all-reduces move hidden-size vectors (4,096 values)
LoRA outputs are compressed to 4 bits before sending
Adapters skip the attention block entirely
blocks.explain: Each LoRA collective carries the r-dimensional intermediate, and both sides scale with (N - 1)/N, so the ratio is 9r/(4h) per layer: 0.88% at rank 16 for the 7B shape. The last LoRA result is added into the base partial sum and needs no collective of its own.

blocks.question: A 4-GPU deployment serves rank-64 adapters with long prompts, and profiling shows the LoRA shrink and expand kernels are a large share of each step. What does vLLM's documentation suggest trying?
options: Lower the tensor-parallel size to 1
Raise max_lora_rank to 256
Enable --fully-sharded-loras, which splits every adapter matrix instead of replicating half
Merge all adapters into the base
blocks.explain: The default mode replicates A on column layers and B on row layers, so every GPU repeats that work. Fully sharded splits it N ways for a few small collectives, which the docs say is likely faster at high sequence length, max rank or TP size.

lessons.title: Multi-LoRA in vLLM and LoRAX, and the cost model

blocks.md: These ideas now ship in open-source servers. In **vLLM** you start the server with LoRA enabled and register adapters; a request then names an adapter as if it were a model, and vLLM batches it with base-model requests and other adapters. Internally, vLLM's LoRA layers go through a component called the Punica wrapper, with Triton kernels named `lora_shrink` and `lora_expand`.

blocks.code:
vllm serve meta-llama/Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct \
    --enable-lora \
    --lora-modules sql-lora=jeeejeee/llama32-3b-text2sql-spider \
    --max-loras 4 --max-lora-rank 16 --max-cpu-loras 32

curl http://localhost:8000/v1/completions \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d '{"model": "sql-lora", "prompt": "San Francisco is a", "max_tokens": 7}'
blocks.caption: Adapted from the vLLM LoRA docs. The request picks the adapter through the model field.

blocks.md:
The knobs map onto the earlier lessons:
- `max_loras`: how many different adapters can be in one batch (default 1 in current source).
- `max_lora_rank`: the largest rank allowed (default 16 in current source).
- `max_cpu_loras`: how many adapters to keep cached in CPU memory; must be at least `max_loras`.

With `VLLM_ALLOW_RUNTIME_LORA_UPDATING=True`, the server also exposes `/v1/load_lora_adapter` and `/v1/unload_lora_adapter`. The docs warn this carries security risks and belongs only in isolated, trusted environments.

blocks.title: A request for an adapter in a vLLM-style server (simplified)

scenes.caption: An operator registers an adapter at runtime (only with runtime updating enabled).
A request names the adapter in the model field. The scheduler needs it in one of the max_loras GPU slots before the request can join a batch.

add.label: copy A, B into free slot

scenes.caption: The request decodes in a mixed batch with base-model requests and other adapters; tokens stream back.

blocks.md: One implementation detail explains a docs warning. In vLLM's source, each LoRA-wrapped linear layer allocates its adapter buffers up front with shape `(max_loras,1,max_lora_rank,input_size)` for A, that is, max_loras slots of max_lora_rank rows by the layer's input width, and the matching shape for B, and copies a smaller adapter into the top-left corner of a slot. Memory is therefore reserved for `max_loras` adapters at `max_lora_rank`, whatever the real ranks are. The docs advise setting `max_lora_rank` to the largest rank you actually serve.

blocks.title: Reserved LoRA slot memory, 7B shape, max_loras = 4

scenes.caption: Computed from the slot shapes for all seven linear layers of a 32-layer, 4096-wide model in 16-bit: 0.32 GB at rank 16. Simplified: ignores embedding and head adapters.

If every real adapter has rank 16 but you set 256, the slots take 5.12 GB, of which 4.8 GB is padding (the adapters fill only 0.32 GB), memory the KV cache could have used. S-LoRA's rank-sized pages avoid this.

blocks.md: **LoRAX** (LoRA eXchange, from Predibase) is a server built for this use case, forked from Hugging Face's text-generation-inference. Its docs list: dynamic adapter loading per request from the Hugging Face Hub, Predibase or a filesystem; heterogeneous continuous batching that packs requests for different adapters into one batch; adapter exchange scheduling that prefetches and offloads adapters between GPU and CPU; and Punica's SGMV kernel. Launcher flags such as `--max-active-adapters` and `--adapter-cycle-time-s` control how many adapters sit on the GPU and how often they are exchanged. Its GitHub repository has since been archived (read-only), so treat LoRAX as a reference design; vLLM and SGLang are the maintained servers.

LoRAX can also merge several adapters into one for a single request (linear, TIES and DARE merging). The serving use is composition: apply a task adapter and a style adapter together without training a combined one. How the merging methods work, and why they can lose quality, is taught in the LoRA course's lesson on composing adapters.

A cost checklist for a multi-LoRA deployment, all from this course:
1. **Weights**: one base, plus adapter size x number resident (80 MB per rank-16 all-linear adapter for a 7B model).
2. **KV trade**: each resident adapter displaces KV cache (about 152 tokens' worth at that size).
3. **Bandwidth**: each distinct adapter in a batch adds its bytes to every decode step, in proportion to rank.
4. **Cold starts**: a miss costs a host-to-GPU copy (milliseconds) or a disk or network fetch (longer); the next lesson covers the fixes.
5. **Merge** when one adapter dominates; **unmerged** when many are active or the base is quantized.
6. **Several GPUs**: adapters are sharded with the base, and `fully_sharded_loras` trades collectives for memory.
7. **Prefix cache**: cached KV blocks are keyed by adapter (the prefix-caching course), so a shared system prompt is cached once per adapter, not once per server.

Measure your own adapter mix. Punica and S-LoRA both show that results depend on popularity: identical, skewed (a few hot adapters), or distinct (every request different). Hot adapters can stay resident; the long tail can be loaded on demand.

blocks.question: You serve adapters of rank 8 and 16 with vLLM but set --max-lora-rank 256. What is the main consequence?
options: Requests fail because ranks must match exactly
Adapters are automatically retrained at rank 256
Throughput improves because larger slots are faster
GPU memory is reserved for rank-256 slots, wasting space that the KV cache could use
blocks.explain: vLLM preallocates each of the max_loras slots at max_lora_rank and pads smaller adapters into them. The docs warn that setting it much higher than needed wastes memory and can hurt performance.

blocks.question: Traffic is 95% for one adapter, with a long tail of 300 rarely used adapters. Which design fits best?
options: A multi-LoRA server that keeps the hot adapter resident and loads tail adapters on demand from CPU memory
Merge all 300 into separate model copies
Merge-and-swap on a single GPU for all traffic
Serve only the base model
blocks.explain: The tail is what makes separate or swapped deployments expensive. A multi-LoRA server batches everything over one base, keeps the popular adapter in GPU memory, and fetches rare ones on demand. A dedicated merged copy for the hot adapter can still make sense if its latency is critical.

blocks.question: Which statement about LoRAX matches its documentation?
options: It requires all adapters to be merged before serving
It only supports one adapter per GPU
It batches requests for different adapters together and swaps adapters between GPU and CPU memory
It replaces the base model with a quantized adapter
blocks.explain: LoRAX documents heterogeneous continuous batching (different adapters in one batch) and adapter exchange scheduling (prefetch and offload between GPU and CPU), using Punica's SGMV kernel.

lessons.title: Many GPUs, many tenants: placement, cold starts and fairness

blocks.md: Picture 4 GPUs, each running the same 7B base with batches of up to 32, and a stream of requests for 500 adapters. A **router** in front decides which GPU, or **replica**, each request joins. Three problems appear that one GPU never had: where to send each request (and when to move it), what to do when its adapter is not loaded (a **cold start**), and how to keep one busy tenant from starving the rest.

Punica's scheduler answers the first with **consolidation**. It sends a new request to the GPU with the *largest* current batch that still has room: below the maximum batch size (32 on their A100s, picked to stay in the latency sweet spot) and with enough free memory for the request's KV cache. When every GPU is full, requests queue in first-come, first-served order. The effect: busy GPUs stay busy, lightly loaded ones drain, and idle ones stay idle and can be handed back to the cloud. The router ignores which adapter a request uses, because SGMV batches mixed adapters cheaply and a load takes milliseconds.

Requests grow, so a GPU can run out of KV space mid-generation. Punica then **migrates** the newest request on that GPU, which preserves first-come, first-served order. It does not copy the KV cache: the target GPU runs a prefill over the original prompt plus every token generated so far, rebuilding the cache. Punica cites the PagedAttention paper's finding that recomputation is as fast as moving the cache, or faster, in most cases.

blocks.title: Punica migrates request R3 from GPU 1 to GPU 2 (Figure 5)

scenes.caption: GPU 1 has no KV space left. The scheduler cancels the newest request there, R3.
GPU 1 finishes its current step, frees R3's KV cache and drops the token it just produced for R3. Right after cancelling, the scheduler adds R3 to GPU 2.
GPU 2 prefills the prompt plus the tokens generated so far, rebuilding R3's cache, then resumes streaming. The client only sees a short pause.

blocks.md: **dLoRA** (Wu et al., at OSDI 2024, the USENIX operating systems conference) adds two things. Inside each replica it switches per iteration between merged and unmerged modes: in unmerged mode it finds the adapter with the most waiting requests, and if that adapter's share of the first-come batch exceeds a threshold $\alpha_{switch}$ it merges that adapter and runs only its requests; in merged mode, if the share falls below $\beta_{switch}$, it unmerges. A switch costs a $BA$ matmul and an add or subtract over the base weights, so it must pay for itself over the following iterations.

blocks.prompt: dLoRA's own example: switching to merged mode costs 100 ms, a merged iteration 50 ms, an unmerged one 100 ms. Over 3 iterations, which wins, and after how many iterations does switching break even?
blocks.reveal: Unmerged: 3 x 100 = **300 ms**. Switch then merged: 100 + 3 x 50 = **250 ms**, so switching wins. Each merged iteration saves 50 ms, so the 100 ms switch is repaid after 2 iterations and only profits from the third. Because nobody knows how long a burst will last, dLoRA tunes $\alpha_{switch}$ from history: if recent merged periods ran faster it lowers the threshold, otherwise it raises it.

blocks.md: Across replicas, dLoRA dispatches each request to the replica with the shortest estimated pending time: the time to load its adapter if that replica lacks it, plus the expected queueing there. Because output lengths are unknown, load still drifts apart, so dLoRA also solves an integer program that moves requests and copies adapters between replicas, run only when a replica crosses a memory or queueing threshold and only among the K most and least loaded replicas. Like Punica it moves a request as tokens and rebuilds its state. The paper reports up to 57.9x the throughput of a vLLM baseline that ran one merged model per instance (vLLM had no multi-LoRA support then) and 1.8x lower average latency than S-LoRA on its workloads.

Does routing by adapter help? A script compares three routers for 128 concurrent requests on 4 GPUs, with adapter popularity Zipf with exponent 1 (adapter $i$ drawn with probability proportional to $1/i$ over 500 adapters; the top one gets 14.7% of traffic), averaged over 5,000 draws:
- **Round robin**: 32 per GPU, 23.6 distinct adapters per GPU, so 1.88 GB of adapter reads per step, 14.0% on top of the 13.5 GB base.
- **Affinity** (adapter $i$ always on GPU $(i - 1)$ mod 4): 17.4 distinct (10.3%), but GPU 0 gets 33% of all traffic, 43 requests on average for 32 slots.
- **Hybrid** (the 8 hottest adapters on every GPU, the tail pinned): 21.0 distinct, busiest GPU 36.7.

blocks.title: Routing 128 requests over 4 GPUs, 500 adapters, Zipf exponent 1

scenes.caption: Distinct adapters per GPU per step (simulated, 5,000 draws). Affinity reads about a quarter fewer adapter bytes, but the saving is 1.88 versus 1.39 GB per step.
Requests on the busiest GPU (32 slots each). Affinity puts the hottest adapter's whole share on one GPU: about 43 requests, so 11 queue while other GPUs have room.

blocks.md: **Cold starts.** Systems keep adapters in host memory and copy them in on demand, so a request for a non-resident adapter waits. CaraServe (Li et al. 2024) measured single loads from a few to tens of milliseconds depending on adapter size, and, because a newcomer's prefill blocks the in-flight decodes under continuous batching, cold starts took on average 10%, 16% and 20% of request serving time at 3, 6 and 9 requests per second (Llama2-7B, 512 rank-64 adapters, skewed popularity). Punica copies asynchronously so other rows keep decoding; S-LoRA prefetches from the queue. CaraServe starts the new request's LoRA work on the CPU during the copy, while the GPU runs the base, then hands over once the adapter lands.

blocks.title: A request whose adapter is not on the GPU (illustrative)

scenes.caption: Assumed costs: 20 ms to copy a large adapter (the 80 MB one takes about 2.5 ms), 30 ms of prefill. Blocking load: nothing for R2 starts until the copy ends, so its first token comes at 50 ms.
Asynchronous copy (Punica): the GPU keeps decoding the current batch during the copy, and R2 joins afterwards. Others no longer wait, but R2's first token is still at 50 ms.

CPU-assisted (CaraServe): the GPU starts R2's base prefill at once while the CPU computes the LoRA term until the copy lands. First token near 32 ms. Simplified: assumes the CPU keeps pace, with 2 ms of hand-over.

blocks.md: CaraServe also schedules by **rank**. Its profiling found that the cost of a mixed batch follows the largest rank in it for Punica's BGMV kernel (batched gather matrix-vector, which gathers each row's adapter) and the average rank for S-LoRA's MBGMV, so it routes each request to the server whose predicted added latency and SLO violations are lowest. It reports up to 1.4x lower average latency than S-LoRA. Servers expose the same levers. SGLang's `--max-loras-per-batch` sets the GPU adapter slots (base-model requests also take one when present), `--max-loaded-loras` the host cache, `--lora-eviction-policy` picks LRU or FIFO, pinned adapters never leave the GPU (at most one fewer than the slots), and `--enable-lora-overlap-loading` overlaps copies with compute. It is off by default: it can split multi-adapter prefill batches and raise latency when loads are already fast.

**Fairness.** First come, first served gives each tenant service in proportion to how much it sends, so one tenant's burst of long jobs delays everyone. The fair-share fix, the Virtual Token Counter (VTC), admits from the client that has received the least weighted service; it is taught in the LLM inference systems course's lesson Who goes next. Multi-LoRA adds a conflict: adapter clustering, affinity and dLoRA's merged mode all favour the hot adapter's requests, which is the opposite of fair. dLoRA guards against starvation with credits: every adapter starts with the same credit, a request served out of first-come order passes credit to the adapter it skipped, and an adapter whose credit passes a threshold is served first.

Routing every request for an adapter to one GPU looks efficient, since fewer distinct adapters per batch means fewer bytes. Under skewed popularity it concentrates the hottest tenant on one replica. Replicate hot adapters, pin only the tail, and let migration or a load-aware dispatcher handle the rest.

At cluster scale, multi-LoRA serving is a placement problem: consolidate load (Punica), switch merged and unmerged as traffic skews (dLoRA), hide adapter loads (prefetch, async or CPU-assisted prefill), and schedule for fairness across tenants, not only for throughput.

blocks.question: A dLoRA replica is unmerged. In the current queue, 90% of the first-come batch is for adapter S, and bursts for S usually last many iterations. What should the replica do?
options: Stay unmerged: merging is only for single-adapter servers
Migrate every request for S to another replica
Evict adapter S to make room for the tail
Merge S and run its requests, because the share is above the switching threshold and the switch cost is repaid over the burst
blocks.explain: A merged iteration skips the LoRA add-on and batches only S, so when S dominates and the burst lasts, the one-off cost of BA plus the weight update is repaid. When S's share drops below beta_switch, dLoRA unmerges and returns to mixed batches.

blocks.question: Two tenants share a multi-LoRA server. Tenant X submits 500 long batch jobs at once; tenant Y sends a chat request every few seconds. Under first-come, first-served, what happens to Y?
options: Y waits behind X's backlog, because FCFS serves tenants in proportion to what they submit
Y is served first because its requests are shorter
Nothing: SGMV gives each adapter an equal share of every batch
Y's adapter is merged into the base to protect it
blocks.explain: FCFS knows only arrival order, so X's burst fills the queue ahead of Y. A per-client fair scheduler such as VTC admits from the least-served client instead, and adapter-level credits (dLoRA) keep hot adapters from starving cold ones.

lessons.title: Build it and size it: a mixed-adapter layer and a capacity plan

blocks.md: Time to build the core of the course in a few lines of NumPy, on a CPU. One linear layer of width 256, four rank-16 adapters, and a batch of 8 rows whose adapters are B, A, D, A, C, B, A, D (indices 1, 0, 3, 0, 2, 1, 0, 3): the batch from the SGMV lesson. Two versions compute $XW_0$ plus each row's own $xAB$. **BGMV-style** gathers each row's $A$ and $B$ and multiplies row by row. **SGMV-style** sorts rows by adapter and runs one matmul per segment. Both are checked against the reference: each row times its merged weight $W_0 + A_aB_a$.

blocks.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
h, r, n_ad, rows = 256, 16, 4, 8
W0 = rng.standard_normal((h, h), dtype=np.float32) / 16
A = rng.standard_normal((n_ad, h, r), dtype=np.float32) / 16  # S-LoRA layout: x @ A @ B
B = rng.standard_normal((n_ad, r, h), dtype=np.float32) / 16
x = rng.standard_normal((rows, h), dtype=np.float32)
idx = np.array([1, 0, 3, 0, 2, 1, 0, 3])          # adapter of each row

def bgmv(x, idx):                                  # gather per row
    v = np.einsum('bh,bhr->br', x, A[idx])         # shrink: each row reads its own A
    return x @ W0 + np.einsum('br,brh->bh', v, B[idx])   # expand

def sgmv(x, idx):                                  # sort, then one matmul per segment
    order = np.argsort(idx, kind='stable')
    xs, ids = x[order], idx[order]
    s = np.flatnonzero(np.r_[True, ids[1:] != ids[:-1], True])  # segment starts + end
    y = xs @ W0
    for lo, hi in zip(s[:-1], s[1:]):
        a = ids[lo]
        y[lo:hi] += xs[lo:hi] @ A[a] @ B[a]
    out = np.empty_like(y); out[order] = y        # undo the sort
    return out, s

ref = np.stack([x[i] @ (W0 + A[a] @ B[a]) for i, a in enumerate(idx)])  # merged, per row
yb = bgmv(x, idx); ys, s = sgmv(x, idx)
print("segments s =", s.tolist())
print("max |bgmv - merged| =", f"{np.abs(yb - ref).max():.1e}")
print("max |sgmv - merged| =", f"{np.abs(ys - ref).max():.1e}")
per = (h*r + r*h) * 2                              # bytes of one adapter pair, 16-bit
print("adapter bytes read: bgmv", len(idx)*per, " sgmv", len(set(idx.tolist()))*per)
blocks.caption: Runs on CPU with NumPy (OMP_NUM_THREADS=2). Uses S-LoRA's layout, x @ A @ B.

blocks.md:
Real output:
```
segments s = [0, 3, 5, 6, 8]
max |bgmv - merged| = 1.9e-06
max |sgmv - merged| = 1.9e-06
adapter bytes read: bgmv 131072  sgmv 65536
```
Both match the merged weights to float32 rounding (the last digits depend on the BLAS library NumPy uses; an OpenBLAS build printed 2.9e-06, and some macOS OpenBLAS builds also print harmless RuntimeWarnings from matmul), so the unmerged form really computes each row's own fine-tune. The segment list is the one from the SGMV lesson. The gather version materializes one copy of the adapter weights per row (8 pairs), the segmented version touches each distinct adapter once (4 pairs): the I/O term $n\,h_ih_o$ of Punica's roofline, seen in miniature.

blocks.title: Inside sgmv(): sort, find segments, one matmul per adapter
blocks.code:
order = np.argsort(idx, kind='stable')
xs, ids = x[order], idx[order]
s = np.flatnonzero(np.r_[True, ids[1:] != ids[:-1], True])
y = xs @ W0
for lo, hi in zip(s[:-1], s[1:]):
    a = ids[lo]
    y[lo:hi] += xs[lo:hi] @ A[a] @ B[a]
out = np.empty_like(y); out[order] = y

scenes.caption: A stable sort by adapter id. Rows 1, 3 and 6 use adapter 0 (A), so they come first, in their original order.
A segment starts wherever the id changes, plus one end marker: the boundary list s from Punica's definition.
The base matmul runs once for all rows. Row order does not matter to it.
Segment 0: three rows times adapter 0's A (256 x 16) then B (16 x 256). Each adapter's weights are read once per segment.
The last segment, adapter 3, rows 6 and 7. A GPU kernel launches all segments at once instead of looping.
Scatter the rows back to arrival order, so each request gets its own output. The error's last digits depend on the BLAS library.

blocks.md: On a GPU you would not write this loop. vLLM's offline API takes one `LoRARequest(name, unique id, path)` per prompt and batches them through its Punica-wrapper kernels. A sketch mixing two adapters in one `generate` call follows the docs' pattern; it needs a GPU and was not run here.

blocks.code:
# Not run here (needs an NVIDIA GPU). Pattern from the vLLM LoRA docs.
from vllm import LLM, SamplingParams
from vllm.lora.request import LoRARequest

llm = LLM(model="meta-llama/Llama-2-7b-hf", enable_lora=True,
          max_loras=2, max_lora_rank=16, max_cpu_loras=8)
sql = LoRARequest("sql", 1, "/adapters/sql")
chat = LoRARequest("chat", 2, "/adapters/chat")
prompts = ["Write SQL: list all users", "Hi, how are you?"]
outs = llm.generate(prompts, SamplingParams(max_tokens=64),
                    lora_request=[sql, chat])   # one per prompt
for o in outs:
    print(o.outputs[0].text)
blocks.caption: generate accepts a list of LoRA requests paired with the prompts. With max_loras=1, vLLM's multi-LoRA example notes the second adapter's requests run after the first's finish.

blocks.md: Now size a deployment. Workload: one A100 80GB, the 7B base, 500 rank-16 adapters with Zipf popularity (exponent 1), batches of 32, about 1,024 tokens of context per sequence. Assume 72 GB usable after activations and runtime (an assumption, not a vLLM default). The script below computes the distinct adapters a batch of 32 needs, the slots and KV pool that follow, and a step time from the basics course's bandwidth model: bytes read per step over 2.039 TB/s.

blocks.code:
import numpy as np
GB, MiB = 1e9, 2**20
L, h, f = 32, 4096, 11008                      # Llama-2-7B shape
base = 6.74e9 * 2                              # 16-bit weights
adapter = lambda r: L * r * (4*2*h + 3*(h + f)) * 2   # all 7 linear layers
kv_tok = 2 * L * h * 2                         # K and V, 16-bit: 0.5 MiB
usable, batch, ctx, n, bw = 72 * GB, 32, 1024, 500, 2.039e12   # assumptions

p = 1 / np.arange(1, n + 1); p /= p.sum()      # Zipf, exponent 1
distinct = (1 - (1 - p) ** batch).sum()        # expected adapters per batch
sims = [len(set(np.random.default_rng(s).choice(n, batch, p=p))) for s in range(5000)]
max_loras = 32                                 # covers p99 of distinct
slots = max_loras * adapter(16)
kv = usable - base - slots
print(f"adapter {adapter(16)/1e6:.1f} MB = {adapter(16)/kv_tok:.0f} tokens of KV")
print(f"distinct per batch: mean {distinct:.1f}, p99 {np.percentile(sims, 99):.0f}")
print(f"slots {slots/GB:.2f} GB, KV pool {kv/GB:.2f} GB = {kv/kv_tok:,.0f} tokens "
      f"= {kv/kv_tok/ctx:.0f} sequences of {ctx}")
step = lambda d: (base + d * adapter(16) + batch * ctx * kv_tok) / bw * 1e3
print(f"step {step(0):.2f} ms without LoRA, {step(distinct):.2f} ms with; "
      f"{batch/step(0)*1e3:,.0f} vs {batch/step(distinct)*1e3:,.0f} tokens/s")
print(f"all {n} adapters in host RAM: {n*adapter(16)/GB:.0f} GB; "
      f"one host-to-GPU copy at 32 GB/s: {adapter(16)/32e9*1e3:.1f} ms")

Real output:
```
adapter 80.0 MB = 152 tokens of KV
distinct per batch: mean 23.6, p99 29
slots 2.56 GB, KV pool 55.96 GB = 106,738 tokens = 104 sequences of 1024
step 15.04 ms without LoRA, 15.96 ms with; 2,128 vs 2,005 tokens/s
all 500 adapters in host RAM: 40 GB; one host-to-GPU copy at 32 GB/s: 2.5 ms
```
The settings follow. A batch of 32 under this popularity needs about 24 adapters at once, so `max_loras` 8 would hold most of the tail back; 32 covers the 99th percentile for 2.56 GB, about 4,900 tokens of KV. `max_lora_rank` 16 matches the adapters. `max_cpu_loras` 500 keeps every adapter one 2.5 ms copy away instead of a disk read. The 24 distinct adapters add about 6% to each step in this model.

blocks.md: Then measure. S-LoRA's synthetic workload has four knobs: $n$ adapters, a total rate $R$ requests per second, burstiness $cv$ (the coefficient of variation of the gaps between arrivals; 1 is Poisson-like, larger is burstier) and a popularity exponent $\alpha$, with prompt and output lengths uniform in [8, 512]. Its defaults for a 7B base on an A100 80GB are $n = 200$, $\alpha = 1$, $R = 10$, $cv = 1$, over 5 minutes. The metrics are throughput, average request latency, average first-token latency and **SLO attainment**, the share of requests whose first token arrives within 6 seconds.

blocks.code:
import numpy as np

def slora_trace(n, alpha, rate, cv, duration, lo=8, hi=512, seed=42):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    m = int(rate * duration)
    adapter = (rng.power(alpha, m) * n).astype(int)        # density alpha*x^(alpha-1)
    gaps = rng.gamma(1 / cv**2, cv**2 / rate, m)            # mean 1/rate, CV = cv
    t = np.cumsum(gaps)
    return t, adapter, rng.integers(lo, hi, m), rng.integers(lo, hi, m)

for alpha in (1.0, 0.3, 0.1):
    t, a, inp, out = slora_trace(n=200, alpha=alpha, rate=10, cv=1, duration=300)
    share = np.bincount(a, minlength=200) / len(a)
    print(f"alpha {alpha}: {len(a)} requests over {t[-1]:.0f} s, "
          f"adapters used {len(set(a))}, top-adapter share {share.max():.1%}, "
          f"top-10 share {np.sort(share)[-10:].sum():.1%}")
t, a, _, _ = slora_trace(200, 1.0, 10, 4, 300)
g = np.diff(t); print(f"cv=4: gap mean {g.mean():.3f} s, CV {g.std()/g.mean():.2f}")
blocks.caption: Follows S-LoRA's benchmarks/trace.py: the adapter is the integer part of n times X, X from NumPy's power distribution; gaps are Gamma with shape 1/cv^2 and mean 1/rate. Runs on CPU.

blocks.md:
Real output:
```
alpha 1.0: 3000 requests over 287 s, adapters used 200, top-adapter share 0.9%, top-10 share 8.0%
alpha 0.3: 3000 requests over 287 s, adapters used 200, top-adapter share 19.6%, top-10 share 40.6%
alpha 0.1: 3000 requests over 287 s, adapters used 188, top-adapter share 58.3%, top-10 share 74.1%
cv=4: gap mean 0.107 s, CV 4.12
```
Read the code before trusting the name: in S-LoRA's generator $\alpha = 1$ is *uniform* popularity, and smaller $\alpha$ is more skewed, the opposite of a Zipf exponent. To replay your own traffic, S-LoRA samples $R \times D$ requests from a log and rescales their timestamps into $[0, D]$; keep each request's adapter and lengths.

"Power-law popularity with exponent alpha" means different things in different papers. S-LoRA's alpha = 1 is uniform, Punica's Zipf-1.5 makes each adapter 1.5 times as popular as the next, and this lesson's Zipf exponent 1 gives the top adapter 14.7%. Compare results only after converting to the same quantity, such as the top-10 share.

A mixed-adapter layer is a base matmul plus a gathered low-rank product per row. Size a deployment from the workload: distinct adapters per batch sets max_loras, adapter rank sets the bytes per step, host memory sets max_cpu_loras, and a replayed trace with SLO attainment tells you whether it holds.

blocks.question: Under the lesson's workload (batch 32, 500 adapters, Zipf exponent 1), you set max_loras to 8 to save memory. What happens?
options: Nothing: the scheduler merges the extra adapters
Throughput rises because fewer adapter bytes are read
Batches can hold requests for only 8 adapters, so requests for the long tail wait even when batch slots are free
vLLM raises max_loras automatically
blocks.explain: A batch of 32 draws about 24 distinct adapters on average. With 8 slots the scheduler can only batch requests whose adapters are loaded, so tail requests queue and the effective batch shrinks. The memory saved is 24 x 80 MB, about 1.9 GB.

blocks.question: You benchmark with S-LoRA's trace generator at its default alpha = 1 and report results for a heavily skewed production workload. What is wrong?
options: alpha = 1 means uniform popularity in that generator, the least skewed case, so the benchmark does not match the workload
alpha = 1 sends all traffic to one adapter
The generator ignores alpha
Nothing: alpha = 1 is the standard Zipf law
blocks.explain: The generator draws X from density alpha x^(alpha - 1) on [0, 1], which is uniform when alpha = 1. Skew appears as alpha shrinks: at 0.1 the top adapter took 58% of requests in the run above. Match the generator's top-k shares to your traffic.
